chunks: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Sharif ibn Sabiq, from Al-Fadl ibn Abi Qurra, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said:
'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): "You would be the finest of servants were it not that you consume from the public treasury and do not work with your own hands."'

He said: So Dawud (peace be upon him) wept for forty mornings. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to iron: 'Soften yourself for My servant Dawud!' And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, softened iron for him, and he used to make a coat of armour every day and sell it for a thousand dirhams. He made three hundred and sixty coats of armour and sold them for three hundred and sixty thousand, and became needless of the public treasury.

key_terms.بَيْتِ الْمَالِ: The public treasury (bayt al-mal) — the collective wealth of the Muslim community administered by the ruler for common welfare. Drawing from it without legitimate cause was considered a moral fault even for a prophet.
key_terms.دِرْع: A coat of chainmail armour (dir). The Quran (21:80; 34:10-11) alludes to God teaching Dawud the craft of armour-making, which this hadith elaborates as a miracle of iron being divinely softened.
key_terms.نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ: An expression of divine praise, excellent is the servant — contrasted here with the caveat about consuming from public funds, illustrating that otherwise exemplary piety is insufficient if accompanied by economic dependence on communal wealth.

ai.seo_question: Why did Prophet Dawud weep for forty days and what miracle allowed him to become financially independent?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) narrates that Prophet Dawud was praised by God as an excellent servant but rebuked for depending on the public treasury without working with his own hands. This teaching, preserved in the chain from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), situates the Prophet-King Dawud as a model of repentance and economic self-reliance: his forty mornings of weeping so moved God's mercy that iron was miraculously softened for him, enabling him to craft and sell armour until he no longer needed public funds. The narrative establishes a norm that even prophets and rulers should earn their livelihood through personal labour rather than drawing on communal wealth.
